Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

we have a key to a small locked shed. inside there are six hand tools with worn handles, one wheelbarrow with a soft tyre, two watering cans, three empty seed trays, and a coil of hose that might have a leak. nobody has checked whether the tools can be repaired. a mains tap is beside the shed, but it is shared with the library grounds team. one neighbour said, “the tap is fine in summer, but it slows to a trickle when everybody is watering.” we don't know if that's a regular problem or just something they remember from one hot week. there is no known electricity at the plots. don't assume we can install a tank or change the tap; we'd need permission for either.

our current cash is about £650, including any seeds, compost, repairs, signs or other supplies for this first stage. we might be able to ask a local shop for donations, but nothing has been promised, so please don't count donated things as available. we have not agreed to monthly fees or a future budget yet. one member can keep receipts, and the group prefers to buy locally where possible. we'd like to avoid spending the whole amount before we know what the soil and the broken equipment need. there is a council contact for the site, but we have only emailed them once and have not received an answer about the boundary fence or what we may attach to it.

we haven't had a soil test. the ground in the plots looks dark in some places and pale and gritty in others, and one corner stays wet a day or two after rain. an older gardener thinks that corner used to be used for storing bags of compost, but they're not certain. we have no information about past pesticide use. please don't treat the soil as safe or unsafe based on those observations alone. tell us what checks or questions should come before growing food in an uncertain area, and show how the rest of the plan could proceed while we wait for answers. we also need to keep the main path clear for a pushchair and for people who use walking sticks. right now a stack of broken edging is partly in the way, and we don't know who left it there.

Focus on what our volunteer group can realistically do over the first twelve weeks, what should happen first, and what can wait. Use the details below; do not assume we are starting with an empty site or that unresolved questions have already been answered.

## Site and group

The allotment is behind a public library on a narrow block between flats and a bus road. It has been established for a long time, but the previous group stopped meeting last autumn. There are eighteen numbered plots, each about two by four metres: eleven are in regular use, three are partly used, and four are mostly weeds and old stakes. The paths are compacted and two spots become muddy after rain.

Eleven adults have offered to help, though availability changes because of shift work and caring duties. Two usually come on Saturday mornings, three can come after work on Tuesdays, and the others are occasional volunteers. Children aged mostly five to twelve visit with their families, but they are not a fixed workforce. Nobody is a trained horticulturist. One member has years of experience with balcony pots, and another used to grow vegetables with a grandparent. Make the instructions usable by newcomers. We speak English together; some members also speak Polish or Somali. Not everyone can attend the same meeting or read a long technical handout.

We can meet for about forty-five minutes every other week. Work sessions can last up to two hours, though some volunteers may only manage half an hour. Include brief tasks that can be shared or handed over, and a basic note-taking method so people who miss a session can catch up. Identify safe ways for children to join with an adult without assigning them essential work.

## Equipment, budget and permissions

A small locked shed holds six hand tools with worn handles, a wheelbarrow with a soft tyre, two watering cans, three empty seed trays and a coil of hose that may leak. No one has checked whether the tools can be repaired. A mains tap beside the shed is shared with the library grounds team. A neighbour said, “the tap is fine in summer, but it slows to a trickle when everybody is watering.” We do not know whether that is a regular issue or a recollection of one hot week. There is no known electricity at the plots. Do not assume we can install a tank or change the tap; either would require permission.

We have about £650 for seeds, compost, repairs, signs and other supplies for this first stage. Donations from a local shop might be possible, but none are promised, so do not count donated items as available. No monthly fees or future budget have been agreed. One member can keep receipts, and we prefer to buy locally where possible. Avoid spending the whole amount before we understand the soil and equipment needs. We have emailed the council contact once but have not received an answer about the boundary fence or what may be attached to it.

## Ground, crops and shared use

We have not had a soil test. The soil looks dark in some places and pale and gritty in others. One corner stays wet for a day or two after rain. An older gardener thinks bags of compost may once have been stored there but is not certain. We have no information about past pesticide use. Do not treat the soil as safe or unsafe based on these observations alone. Explain what checks or questions should come before food is grown in uncertain ground, and how other planning can continue while we wait for answers.

Keep the main path clear for a pushchair and people who use walking sticks. Broken edging is partly blocking it, and we do not know who left it there. The group is considering salad leaves, peas, beans, radishes, herbs and a few flowers that attract pollinators. Some members want tomatoes, but nobody has offered to care for pots during the week. Recommend a manageable range from these suggestions rather than promising every mentioned crop. The group has not decided whether plots will remain individually managed or whether some will be shared; do not decide this for us. Include a fair way to contact previous users of the four neglected plots so they can say whether they want to return, and a way to avoid disputes over those plots.

Be considerate of noise because flats face the site. The library has story time on some Saturday mornings, but we do not know the full schedule. Do not assume that schedule, water access or council permissions are settled.

## Requested plan

Distinguish what volunteers can do themselves from actions that depend on a council reply, a soil check or confirmation from the library. Use stages or weeks across the first twelve weeks, without assuming the weather or dates for responses. Cover:

1. What to inspect and tidy first; safe handling of old stakes and broken edging; checking tools and the hose before buying replacements; and organizing shared task and supply lists. Include a simple spending record and a way to decide when to pause purchases. List questions for the council and library about the fence, water use, access and Saturday scheduling without implying that they have agreed to anything.
2. Uncertain ground and sensible next steps before food crops go in; preparing only plots the group can manage; choosing a modest first set of suggested crops; sowing or planting at a suitable point in the season without assuming an exact date; and watering if the shared tap is limited. Address paths, the wet corner, compost, weeds and pollinator flowers where relevant. Identify missing information rather than filling it in.
3. A week-by-week or staged twelve-week outline, a short supply list with rough priorities rather than invented prices, a fair approach to contacting users of the four neglected plots, and a few signs that would show whether the plan is working or needs to change.

Keep the plan practical and in plain language, not a full planting encyclopedia. Make choices and unanswered questions visible.
